name: A Psychrometric Bound on Atmospheric Water Harvesting: Where Air-Derived Water Can Work, Where It Cannot, and One Design That Respects the Bound
explanation: This blueprint specifies one design only: the night-only, radiatively assisted condensation unit sized in Section 4.3 of the source paper. It is a household atmospheric water harvesting unit that cools humid night air below its dew point on a cold surface, collects the condensate, and uses a sky-facing radiator panel to carry part of the cooling load so that a vapour-compression refrigerator carries only the remainder.

name: A Batch Reverse-Osmosis Cycle Whose Pressure Follows the Osmotic Curve: First-Principles Energy Accounting and a Sized Village Unit
explanation: A village desalination unit whose batch cycle follows the osmotic pressure curve instead of holding big-plant pressures throughout. It serves desalination equipment makers and NGO water suppliers working at village scale.

name: The Electrodialysis–Reverse Osmosis Crossover for Brackish Groundwater: A First-Principles Energy Derivation and a Sized Village Electrodialysis Unit
explanation: This blueprint specifies a small, photovoltaic-powered electrodialysis (ED) unit that desalinates brackish borehole water for a village drinking-water supply. It takes a feed of 2.5 g/L total dissolved salts (expressed as sodium-chloride equivalent) and produces 5 m³ per day of water at 0.5 g/L, operating 20 hours per day.

name: Forward Osmosis Priced Honestly: A Regeneration Bound That Closes the Seawater Claim, and the Fertilizer-Draw Irrigation Design That Survives It
explanation: This blueprint specifies a fertilizer-draw forward osmosis unit that treats brackish groundwater and delivers its diluted draw directly to crops as liquid fertilizer. Water crosses a semipermeable membrane from a brackish feed into a concentrated fertilizer draw.

name: Designing a Fog Collector Instead of Copying One: Droplet-Capture Physics, Shade-Coefficient Optimisation and an Honest Seasonal Yield for an Arid Coastal Climate
explanation: This blueprint specifies a fog water harvesting panel: a vertical mesh panel, 10 m wide by 4 m high (40 m²), erected with its face perpendicular to the fog-bearing wind at an arid coastal site. Fog-laden air passes through two offset layers of woven mesh; droplets strike the fibres by inertial impaction, coalesce, and drain under gravity to a collection gutter along the panel's lower edge, which feeds a downpipe and a storage tank.

name: Freeze Desalination Priced Honestly: Full Accounting of Washing, Brine Entrainment and Refrigeration for Natural and Refrigerated Freezing of Seawater
explanation: This blueprint specifies a shallow-tray array that desalinates seawater by freezing it with ambient winter air, harvesting the ice, washing the harvested ice with a portion of its own product water, and melting the washed ice to a product target of 0.5 g/L from a 35 g/L seawater feed. No refrigerant, compressor, membrane or pressure vessel is used.

name: A Subsurface-Flow Constructed Wetland for a Household Cluster's Greywater, Sized by Removal Kinetics: The Bed Area, the Pathogen Reduction, and the Arid Salt Budget That Decide Its Reuse Class
explanation: This blueprint specifies a horizontal subsurface-flow constructed wetland — a gravel bed planted with emergent vegetation, through which greywater flows below the gravel surface — for a household cluster of 10 people producing 600 L/day of greywater from baths, hand basins, laundry and kitchen sinks, excluding toilet waste. The bed is 12.92 m² in plan, 0.60 m deep, and treats the full cluster flow with no power, no chemical supply and no moving parts.

name: Intermittent Water Supply: The Intrusion Volume per Outage Computed from First Principles, and a Household Break-Tank Design That Defeats It
explanation: This blueprint specifies a single-household break tank for a piped supply that is pressurised only in two windows per day. Water from the main fills the tank only while the main is pressurised.

name: Locating Distribution Leaks by Pressure-Transient Timing on a Network of Low-Cost Loggers: A Method for Plastic-Pipe Networks Where Acoustic Correlation Fails
explanation: A method and logger network that locates leaks in plastic-pipe water networks by timing pressure transients — the approach that works where the standard acoustic method does not. It serves water-utility instrument makers and, through them, municipalities.

name: The Reservoir Is the Sand: Extractable-Storage Accounting, Evaporation Suppression and Worked Sizing for a Sand Dam on a Seasonal River
explanation: This blueprint specifies a sand-storage dam for a village beside a seasonal river: a low impermeable wall built across a sandy riverbed in small staged lifts, so that flood flows deposit coarse sand behind it, season by season, until the accumulated sand body itself becomes the reservoir. Water is stored inside the sand, in the pore space between the grains, and is drawn off through the dry season from an abstraction point upstream of the wall.

name: A Village Chlorination System with No Chemical Supply Chain: Electrolytic Hypochlorite from Salt, Water and Sunlight, Sized End-to-End from Electrochemistry and Chlorine Decay
explanation: A village water-disinfection unit that makes its own chlorine from salt, water, and solar electricity on site. It serves water-treatment equipment makers and NGO water suppliers.

name: A Batch Solar Water Pasteurizer with Counterflow Heat Recovery: Lethality Priced from Thermal Death Kinetics and Daily Output Sized from Insolation
explanation: This blueprint specifies an institutional batch solar water pasteurizer sized for 200 litres of treated water per day — the school unit of the source paper. A charge of 50.0 litres of raw water is preheated in a counterflow heat exchanger by the previous treated charge, heated by a glazed flat-plate solar collector to 65 °C, held at that temperature for 10 minutes, and then discharged through the same exchanger into a closed treated-water storage vessel fitted with a tap, while the next raw charge passes through the exchanger in the opposite direction into the batch tank.

name: A Solar-Powered Ultraviolet-C LED Disinfection Unit for a Village Standpipe, Sized on the Minimum Delivered Dose in Turbid Water
explanation: A UV water-treatment unit sized on the 5th-percentile dose rather than the average dose. It serves water-treatment equipment makers whose customers need disinfection they can stand behind.

name: A Rain-Ingress Witness for Hand-Dug Wells and Boreholes: Mixing-Derived Detection Floors, Alarm Behaviour and Lead Time from a Low-Cost Conductivity and Temperature Logger
explanation: This blueprint specifies a well rain-ingress warning instrument: a submersible logger, suspended in a hand-dug well or a borehole, that records temperature-compensated electrical conductivity (EC) and temperature every 10 minutes and raises an alarm when storm-driven surface water has entered the well in a quantity the mixing physics says the sensors can reliably distinguish from ordinary variation. After a storm, surface water enters wells through cracked aprons, unsealed covers and flooded wellheads, and a household may draw and drink the mixed water before any visible change warns it.

name: Recovering Heat from Compost to Warm a Small Greenhouse: System Design, Heat Production Curve, and the Pile Mass Below Which the Plumbing Is Not Worth Installing
explanation: A closed water loop that recovers metabolic heat from a compost pile and delivers it, through a buffer tank, to a small propagation greenhouse at night. A high-density polyethylene coil buried in the pile absorbs heat continuously; a small circulator moves the water to a 1,000 litre insulated buffer tank; the buffer discharges to the greenhouse heating circuit during the 10-hour night, when the seedlings need the heat.

name: A Solar-Regenerated Desiccant Dryer for One Tonne of Smallholder Grain: Water Budget, Sizing and Failure Limits
explanation: A solar-regenerated desiccant dryer that pulls harvest moisture out of grain before mould takes it, using silica gel regenerated by a solar collector. It serves agricultural-equipment manufacturers selling to smallholder regions.

name: An Evaporative Cooling Store for a Village Produce Market: Design, Simulated Performance Across Climates, and the Humidity Failure Line
explanation: A market-scale evaporative cooling store with no electrical power, built from fired brick, charcoal and water. Two brick skins form a cavity filled with coarse charcoal; the cavity is kept wet by a gravity drip line from a raised tank.

name: Gravity-Fed Drip Irrigation from a Raised Tank Without a Pump: A Low-Head Design for a 0.1 Hectare Plot, Its Water Budget and Its Uniformity Limits
explanation: A drip-irrigation kit fed by a tank on a 2.00-metre stand, needing no pump and no power. It serves irrigation-kit manufacturers selling to smallholders.

name: Oxygen-Scavenger Sachet Sizing for Hermetic Grain Storage: A First-Principles Oxygen Budget and Design Rule
explanation: Hermetic grain storage holds oxygen low so that stored-product insects cannot survive or reproduce. An iron-based oxygen-scavenger sachet placed inside the sealed store accelerates and guarantees the drawdown of oxygen.

name: Capturing the Nitrogen That Escapes from Stored Manure: An Acid-Scrubbed Vent for a Covered Store, Its Nitrogen Budget and Its Break-Even Herd Size
explanation: An acid-scrubbed vent for covered manure stores that captures ammonia nitrogen as fertiliser instead of losing it to the air. It serves agricultural-equipment manufacturers and dairy cooperatives' equipment suppliers.

name: A Phase-Change Cold Box for the Last Mile Without a Grid: Computed Sizing, Hold Times, and Recharge for the +4 °C Cargo Class
explanation: A passive cold box for the last leg between a farm, clinic or district store and a village, where there is no refrigeration in transit and no power on the vehicle. The box is a 100 mm expanded polystyrene (EPS) container cooled by sealed phase-change panels that melt at 5.0 °C, inside the 2–8 °C cargo band of the +4 °C cargo class.

name: A Pond-and-Field Nutrient Loop, Closed by Arithmetic or Not at All: A Full Nitrogen and Phosphorus Budget for a 0.2 ha Fish Pond Serving 0.5 ha of Crops
explanation: The unit is one integrated pond-and-field system on 0.70 ha in total, as stated in the source paper: 1. 0.20 ha surface, mean depth 1.5 m, stocked with Nile tilapia.

name: Edge-of-Field Runoff Capture Sized from First Principles: A Woodchip Denitrification Bioreactor for 20 Hectares of Drained Cropland
explanation: The unit treats tile drainage from a 20 ha (200,000 m²) field of drained cropland at the field edge, before the drainage reaches the ditch or watercourse. Inlet water-control structure.

name: A Combined Solar Tunnel Dryer and Desiccant-Bead Store for Village Seed Saving: Design, Budgets, and Failure Floor
explanation: A village seed station that treats drying and storage as one problem, in batches of one tonne of seed grain. In the first stage a solar tunnel dryer of 24 m² brings the batch from 20% moisture (wet basis) to 12% without the seed temperature ever exceeding 40 °C.

name: A Village Solar Dehydrator for a 50 kg Mango Batch: Water Budget, Collector and Airflow Sizing, Drying Time and the Humid-Season Failure Line
explanation: An indirect solar dehydrator that dries one batch of 50 kg of fresh mango per loading. Heated air from a flat-plate solar collector is driven by a small photovoltaic-powered fan through an insulated cabinet holding a stack of ten trays.

name: A No-Electronics Witness Label for Sealed Grain Stores: Integrating Moisture Exposure and Seal Failure on One Passive Card
explanation: A two-channel passive label that turns red when a sealed grain store's seal fails, or when grain was sealed wet. It serves grain-storage and agricultural-input suppliers and food-security programs.

name: A Village Struvite Reactor Turning Source-Separated Urine into Fertiliser: Design and Phosphorus Budget for a 100-Person Community
explanation: A 200-litre batch reactor that recovers phosphorus from urine as struvite fertiliser, sized for a 100-person settlement. It serves sanitation and fertiliser firms and utilities with nutrient-recovery mandates.

name: Household Biogas from the Waste a Family Actually Has: An Honest Energy Budget and a Digester Design for a Six-Person Household with Three Cattle
explanation: This blueprint specifies a household biogas digester for one stated household: - 6 people; - 3 zebu-type cattle, free-grazing by day and kraaled at night; - 2 goats, whose dung is excluded from the feedstock because grazing goats scatter hard pellets that are not practically collectable in useful quantity; - a warm lowland climate, with unheated slurry temperature ranging from 19 °C in the coldest months to 29 °C in the warmest, and cold spells reaching 17 °C. The design is sized backwards from the waste this household actually produces, not from the cooking demand.

name: A Village-Fabricable Chimney Rocket Stove for Clean Cooking: Design, Thermal Performance, Draft, and Indoor Exposure Estimates
explanation: An insulated rocket combustion chamber with a horizontal feed magazine, a pot skirt, and a chimney that carries combustion products out of the kitchen. Wood enters horizontally so that only the ends of the sticks burn.

name: Flywheel Energy Storage at Household and Village Scale: A Reference Design, Its Self-Discharge, and the Duties It Can and Cannot Serve
explanation: The reference machine of the source paper, specified in build-ready form: a hoop-wound carbon-fibre rim of 71.7 kg, 0.64 m in outer diameter (derived: twice the 0.32 m outer radius), spinning at 17,905 revolutions per minute in a vacuum housing on active magnetic bearings, driven by one permanent-magnet motor-generator on the shaft. The rotor stores 2.977 kWh (10.72 MJ) at full speed and delivers 2.009 kWh of electricity through its working speed range (full speed down to half speed, at a discharge efficiency of 0.90), at a round-trip efficiency of 81.0% before any standing loss.

name: An Iron-Air Battery from Abundant Materials for Household and Village Electricity Storage: A First-Principles Design and Cost Test
explanation: A long-duration battery built from iron and air — cheap, abundant materials — sized for storage that lasts days rather than hours. It serves energy-storage manufacturers supplying villages, homes, and small grids that need storage spanning days of low generation.

name: A Village Microgrid Architecture Designed to Survive Its Own Failure Modes
explanation: A four-cluster village microgrid architecture designed so that one failed inverter dims the village instead of blacking it out. It serves mini-grid developers and their equipment suppliers building village electrification.

name: Pico-Hydro Power Without a Dam: A Run-of-Stream Design for a 45-Household Hill Village, Sized to Its Dry Season
explanation: A run-of-stream hydro plant sized to its dry season rather than to its best month, delivering continuous power to a 45-household hill village with no dam and no civil-works budget. It serves rural-electrification contractors, NGO energy suppliers, and regional fabricators.

name: Sand-Battery Thermal Storage for Home Heating: A First-Principles Residential Design for Three Sunless Days in a Cold Climate
explanation: A colder spell, a larger house, or a less well-insulated house raises the required mass, volume, and cost in direct proportion to the load (source paper, Section 2). Do not build this size for a different house without re-running the sizing calculation.

name: A Solar Cooker That Can Cook the Evening Meal: A Panel Cooker with an Oil Thermal Store and a Retained-Heat Basket, Sized for a Family of Five
explanation: The system stores daytime solar heat in oil and cooks the evening meal from stored heat, rather than storing cooked food. It is sized for a family of five (two adults and three children) and for the following stated meal, at an ambient temperature of 28 °C and a cooking temperature of 100 °C: - Pot 1, rice: 0.75 kg dry rice plus 1.50 kg water, 2.25 kg in total, simmered for 30 minutes after reaching boiling point.

name: Battery-Free Solar Refrigeration for Off-Grid Clinics and Homes: A Direct-Drive Design with Ice-Bank Thermal Storage
explanation: A direct-drive solar refrigerator that stores cold in an ice bank instead of storing electricity in a battery. It serves off-grid appliance manufacturers and NGO suppliers running vaccine and food cold chains.

name: Solar Water Pumping That Stores Water, Not Electricity: A Battery-Free Design for Drinking Water and Small-Plot Irrigation
explanation: A direct-drive solar pumping design that stores water in an elevated tank instead of storing electricity in batteries. It serves pump and rural-water suppliers.

name: Waste-Heat Recovery for a Small Intermittent Brick Kiln: Air Preheat and Brick Drying, with Costs, Failure Modes and the Cases Where It Is Not Worth Building
explanation: This blueprint specifies a waste-heat recovery system for one stated case: a small intermittent brick kiln firing 10,000 bricks per batch on a 48-hour firing schedule, as defined in the source paper. The system has three parts, in the order the flue gas meets them: 1.

name: Wake-Steering Fleet Control for a Wind Farm: Designing Against the Spacing and Wake Tax
explanation: A yaw-schedule control method that steers turbine wakes so downwind machines stop stealing each other's wind. It is software and a control schedule; no factory is needed. It serves wind-farm operators and turbine control and SCADA firms.

name: Passive Cooling for Medicine Storage in a Hot Clinic Without Reliable Power: A Radiative, Evaporative and Thermal-Mass Cabinet Design and Its Computed Climate Envelope
explanation: This specification describes how to build and operate a passive cabinet intended to hold medicines at or below 25 °C in a hot clinic without reliable electrical power. The cabinet combines four elements: night-sky radiative cooling from a roof panel, an indirect evaporative jacket operating by day, a water thermal store, and thick insulation.

name: A Passive Phase-Change Vaccine Carrier Sized for 72 Hours at 43 °C: Design and Thermal Model
explanation: A vaccine carrier that holds 2–8 °C on phase-change panels behind a vacuum-panel and foam wall, with no power at all. It serves medical cold-chain manufacturers selling into NGO and ministry-of-health procurement.

name: Household Smoke from Solid-Fuel Cooking: A Low-Cost Chimney Hood Priced by Draft Physics
explanation: This blueprint specifies how to build and install the low-cost chimney hood described in the source paper: a sheet-steel hood over an open fire or simple solid-fuel stove, connected to a vertical flue sized from stack-effect draft physics, with a rotating anti-downdraft cowl and no fan and no electricity. The purpose is to intercept smoke at source, before it mixes into the kitchen, and to carry it outside above the roof ridge.

name: Gravity-Fed Intravenous Infusion Without Pumps, Made Accurate: An Error Budget for the Standard Drip Set and a Constant-Head Mariotte Insert Design
explanation: A small insert, based on the Mariotte constant-head principle, that holds a gravity IV set's flow steady as the bag empties. It rides on the standard set rather than replacing it. It serves medical-supply manufacturers.

name: A Hand-Powered Centrifuge for Blood Separation Where There Is No Power: A Design Envelope Specified from Rotor Physics
explanation: A hand-cranked centrifuge, driven through a 100:1 crank, that separates blood samples with no electricity. It serves laboratory-equipment makers supplying low-resource settings.

name: A Low-Dose Chest Radiography Protocol for Tuberculosis Screening Derived from the Dose-Resolution Trade
explanation: This blueprint specifies an implementation of the low-dose posteroanterior (PA) chest radiography protocol for tuberculosis (TB) screening derived in the source paper. The protocol is intended for population TB screening programmes, as the paper frames it: imaging large numbers of people, most of whom do not have TB, where dose per film therefore matters at population scale even though the dose from a single chest radiograph is small.

name: A Phase-Change Neonatal Warmer for Births Where No Incubator Exists: Design and Lumped Thermal Model
explanation: A phase-change mattress warmer, recharged with hot water, that keeps a newborn warm for hours with no electricity. It serves medical-device firms and NGO medical suppliers working in low-resource maternity care.

name: A Low-Cost Pulse Oximeter with an Honest Accuracy Budget: Design, Error Propagation, and the Accuracy Floor for Triage
explanation: A low-cost pulse oximeter whose accuracy is computed honestly at the corners where cheap devices misread — low perfusion and dark skin. It serves medical-device firms supplying clinics and home care.

name: Oxygen for Childhood Pneumonia Where Cylinders Run Out: A Solar Oxygen Concentrator Sized and Priced from Physics
explanation: A solar array, battery, and concentrator system sized end to end to keep oxygen flowing to a 10-child pneumonia ward, with the sizing done as one system rather than as separate purchases. It serves medical-device firms and NGO medical suppliers equipping off-grid hospitals.

name: Hearing Screening with a Smartphone: An Error Budget and the Protocol It Permits
explanation: This blueprint specifies the implementation of the smartphone pure-tone hearing screening protocol defined in the source paper: a gated, binary, repeat-aware referral screen for moderate-or-worse hearing loss, in which the better-ear four-frequency pure-tone average (PTA) over 500, 1000, 2000 and 4000 Hz is estimated with a phone and its earbuds, and the subject is referred for a clinical audiogram if the estimated PTA is at or above 35 dB HL.

name: Vision Screening with a Smartphone, Bounded by Optics: A Protocol Derived from Display, Camera and Pinhole Limits
explanation: This blueprint specifies the implementation of the smartphone vision screening protocol defined in the source paper: distance visual acuity measured at 2 m against a 6/12 referral threshold, a pinhole step for eyes that fail, and an optional gross photorefraction flag for very large refractive errors only. The scope is the protocol exactly as published: the setting, the distance acuity presentation and its pass/refer rule, the pinhole step and its interpretation, the optional gross photorefraction flag, the optional coarse near check, and the record that must accompany a referral.

name: Solar Water Disinfection Made Quantitative: A UV-A Dose Model for a PET Bottle and a Fixed-Geometry Reflector Backing
explanation: This blueprint specifies the construction of a fixed, non-tracking reflector backing that cradles one horizontal 1.5 L PET bottle for solar water disinfection (SODIS), together with the exposure protocol derived from the source paper's UV-A dose model. One backing unit serves one bottle.

name: Steam Sterilization of Instruments with a Household Pressure Cooker, Priced from Physics — and an Honest Verdict on Solar Sterilization Claims
explanation: This blueprint specifies how to implement the steam sterilization protocol priced in the source paper: saturated steam at 121 °C, at about 103 kPa gauge (15 psi), held for 30 minutes for a wrapped instrument load in a gravity-displacement vessel — a 10 litre household pressure cooker — starting from 25 °C. The scope is the pressure-cooker protocol only.

name: An Ultrasound-First Diagnostic Pathway for Suspected Appendicitis Where No CT Scanner Exists: A Proposed Decision Protocol with a Cohort Model
explanation: This blueprint specifies, for implementation and prospective evaluation, a diagnostic pathway for suspected appendicitis in a district hospital that has basic surgical capability and no CT scanner. In that setting, suspected appendicitis is commonly managed either by clinical judgement alone or by transferring patients to a distant centre for imaging.

name: Ultraviolet Disinfection for Low-Resource Clinics with Honest Dose Budgets: A Priced Specification for Upper-Room Air Treatment and Surface Terminal Disinfection
explanation: This blueprint specifies the installation and implementation of the ultraviolet disinfection systems priced in the source paper for a reference low-resource clinic room of 6.0 × 4.0 × 3.0 m (24 m² floor area, 72 m³ volume). It covers three systems, exactly as specified in the source paper: 1.

name: Airborne-Infection Control in a Low-Resource Clinic Waiting Room, Priced per Dollar: A Model-Derived Ranked Protocol
explanation: This specification describes how to implement, in a low-resource clinic waiting room, the ranked ventilation protocol derived in the source paper. The protocol ranks four ventilation measures by risk reduction per dollar and recommends a combination that holds the modelled infection probability at or below the stated target of 0.05 both when wind is present and when there is no wind.

name: A Water Witness for Clinics: Design and Accuracy Budget of a Low-Cost Photometer for Free Chlorine and Turbidity at the Point of Care
explanation: A small photometer that lets a clinic verify its own water disinfection at the point of care, measuring free chlorine and turbidity. It serves instrument makers and clinic suppliers.

name: A Straw and Rice-Husk Fibre Insulation Panel: Specification and Computed Thermal, Moisture, Cost and Fire-Behaviour Envelope
explanation: This blueprint specifies a semi-rigid, non-loadbearing insulation panel made from agricultural residues: 68% wheat straw fibre, 22% ground rice husk, 6% starch binder and 4% borate treatment by dry mass, at a nominal density of 110 kg per cubic metre. Fibres lie mainly in the plane of the board and trap still air, which provides the insulation.

name: A Flood-Resilient Amphibious Foundation for a Small House: Buoyancy, Guide-Post Loads and Failure Limits
explanation: The foundation lets a single-storey house sit at ground level in dry weather and rise with flood water. The house stands on a watertight hollow buoyant base.

name: A Lashed-Plus-Bolted Bamboo–Timber Joint for Low-Rise Housing: Connector Design and a Computed Shear, Pull-Out and Slip Budget Across Culm Diameter and Moisture
explanation: This blueprint specifies one joint connecting the end region of one bamboo culm (rafter, purlin or joist end) to a timber ledger or tongue 40 mm thick. Two cheap elements share the work.

name: A Confined-Masonry Wall System for One-Storey Stabilised-Earth Housing: Tie-Column and Ring-Beam Layout with a Computed Seismic Shear and Stability Budget
explanation: This blueprint specifies a complete confined-masonry wall system for a one-storey house in stabilised-earth block. Masonry panels are confined on all four sides: reinforced-concrete tie-columns stitch corners, wall ends, intersections and long walls, and a continuous reinforced-concrete ring beam ties the tops of all walls into a single line.

name: A Sacrificial Crack-and-Strain Witness Strip for Small Bridges and Culverts: Design and Computed Threshold Budget
explanation: A passive strip that permanently records peak crack opening, with no power, no electronics, and nothing to maintain. It serves infrastructure-supply firms and municipal road departments through suppliers.

name: A Universal 6% Equal-Split Lime-Cement Formulation for Stabilised-Earth Wall Blocks: A Mix-Selection Computation Balancing Strength, Wet Durability, Embodied Energy and Cost
explanation: A single earth-block recipe — 94% soil, 3% cement, 3% lime — that works across soils from 15% to 40% clay. It serves block-machine makers and housing programs.

name: A Porous Ceramic Evaporator Wall for a Single Room in Arid Housing: Computed Indoor Temperature Reduction, Water Use per Degree, and the Humidity Ceiling
explanation: This blueprint specifies a direct evaporative cooling wall for one room in arid housing. Outside air is drawn by a small fan through a wet, porous ceramic wall into the room.

name: A 20% Rice-Husk Ash, 6% Alkali Formulation for Fly-Ash Geopolymer Wall Blocks: A Formulation Search Priced in Strength, Cost and Carbon per Square Metre of Wall
explanation: A wall-block formulation made from fly ash and rice-husk ash at 6% alkali — waste streams regions currently pay to be rid of. It serves block manufacturers in ash-producing regions.

name: A Household Greywater Treatment and Reuse Bed for Water-Short Settlements: A Sizing Rule and Computed Treatment Budget for a Gravel-and-Reed Subsurface-Flow Design
explanation: The bed is a shallow, lined, horizontal subsurface-flow treatment unit for household greywater — water from washing, bathing and laundry, excluding toilet waste. Greywater first passes through a small pre-filter (a drum or pit of coarse gravel with a removable grease trap) which settles solids and skims grease.

name: A Passive Radiative-Cooling Roof Assembly for Heat-Wave Housing: Computed Cooling Budget and Price per Degree of Indoor Temperature Reduction
explanation: This blueprint specifies a passive roof for a single-storey room of 4 m by 4 m (floor and roof area 16 m², volume 43.2 m³). The roof rejects sunlight by high solar reflectance and radiates heat to the sky through the 8–13 micrometre atmospheric window by high long-wave emissivity.

name: A Rainwater-First Roof and Storage System for a Water-Short Household: Integrated Sizing of Roof, First-Flush Diverter and Tank Against a 450 mm Rainfall Regime
explanation: The system sizes a roof, a first-flush diverter and a storage tank together, as one system, for a five-person household with an essential demand of 100.0 litres per day (20.0 litres per person per day; 36.50 m³ per year) in a rainfall regime of 450.0 mm per year. Rain is caught on a 120.0 m² roof plan, screened at the gutters and downpipes, and the first rain of each event — which carries the dust, droppings and debris accumulated since the previous event — is diverted away from the tank.

name: A Continuous Load-Path Strap-and-Anchor Roof Tie-Down Assembly for Low-Cost Housing: A Computed Uplift Budget and Its Limit Wind Speed
explanation: A continuous strap-and-anchor assembly that keeps the roof-to-ground load path unbroken in storm winds. It serves construction-hardware manufacturers and, secondarily, insurers' mitigation suppliers.

name: A Low-Cost Bridge-Scour Witness Instrument: A Tilt-Node Chain Design and Its Computed Detection Budget
explanation: A chain of tilt nodes fitted at a bridge pier that continuously witnesses riverbed scour — the river quietly digging out the bridge's footing — between inspections. It serves infrastructure-monitoring instrument firms and, through them, road and bridge authorities.

name: A Slope-Failure Witness Network for Informal Hillside Settlements: Node Design and a Computed Warning Budget
explanation: A sensor network that watches hillsides for the moisture and tilt signatures that precede rain-driven slope failure. It serves municipalities, disaster-preparedness NGOs, and sensor-network suppliers protecting hillside settlements.

name: A Solar Desiccation Sanitation Chamber for Households Without Sewers: Computed Moisture-Removal, Pathogen Die-Off, and Safe-Storage Budgets Across Humidity and Season
explanation: The unit is a ventilated, solar-heated drying chamber for a urine-diverting household toilet serving five people. Urine is piped away separately; faecal material falls into the chamber and is spread on shallow stainless mesh trays.

name: A Passive Solar Heating Wall for Cold-Climate Low-Income Housing: A Computed Sizing Rule, Temperature-Lift Budget, and Cost per Degree
explanation: This blueprint specifies a thermal-mass passive solar heating wall of the Trombe class for one room in a poorly insulated house. Sunlight passes through glazing, is absorbed on the dark outer face of a dense concrete mass wall, and is stored in the mass.

name: A Sewerless Thermal Sanitation Unit for a Household: Computed Pathogen Lethality, Energy per Use, and Safe-Handling Intervals for a 2-Litre Batch Design
explanation: A household sanitation unit that makes waste safe by heat — a 2-litre batch at 65 °C for 25 minutes — where no sewer exists. It serves sanitation-equipment firms and NGO sanitation programs.

name: A Household Cookstove Smoke Witness and Chimney-Draft Design Bound: What a Sub-US$20 Carbon Monoxide Witness Can Resolve, and the Flue Dimensions That Keep a Cooking Fire's Smoke Out of the Room
explanation: This blueprint specifies a pair of devices for one kitchen with a flue-connected stove burning a 3.0 kW wood fire: (1) a low-cost carbon monoxide (CO) witness that acts as an alarm, and (2) a natural-draft flue that exhausts the fire's smoke. The flue is the fix; the witness is the instrument that tells the household whether the fix is working, and that keeps working as an alarm in the regimes where no natural-draft flue can.

name: A Flood Witness for Low-Water Road Crossings: Computed Warning Time, Sensor Placement and the False-Closure Trade-Off
explanation: Drivers die at flooded low-water crossings because the water arrives faster than any distant warning, and a driver already at the crossing has no local evidence that the depth is about to become lethal. The lethal decision is made at the crossing, in seconds, with no measurement in front of the driver.

name: What Actually Saves the House: A Priced Cost-Effectiveness Ranking of Ember-Attack Home Hardening, and the Cheapest Bundle That Buys a Stated Survival Probability
explanation: Most homes lost in wildland-urban interface fires are ignited by wind-blown embers, not by a wall of flame. This blueprint specifies, in ranked installation order, the six-measure hardening package for the source reference house — single-storey, 150 m2, replacement value US$450,000, Class A roof already fitted — exposed to a severe ember event with no fire-service suppression, in which the unhardened ignition probability is 0.40 and survival is 0.600.

name: A Household Flood-Safe Store for Settlements That Flood Every Year: Raised-Fixed versus Sealed-Buoyant Design with Computed Elevation, Anchoring, Moisture and Cost Budgets
explanation: In settlements where flooding returns every year, families lose stored grain, seed stock, documents and medicine to water whose arrival is not a surprise. The loss is predictable, so the engineering question is not whether to protect the store, but how high, how sealed, how firmly held down, and at what annual cost — and where protection stops working.

name: A Flood Witness Network for the Settlements That Flood First: Design and a Computed Lead-Time Law for Low-Cost River and Rain Gauge Nodes at US$94 per River Node
explanation: A network of low-cost river nodes that gives flood-prone settlements the warning gauges they have never had. It serves municipalities, disaster agencies, and NGOs protecting settlements that flood first and are gauged last, if at all.

name: A Heat Witness for Outdoor Workers: An Honest Error Bound for Cheap Heat-Stress Estimation
explanation: A $38 sensor with a computed globe correction that estimates workplace heat stress (WBGT) where proper instruments are priced out. It serves safety-equipment manufacturers and large outdoor employers through suppliers.

name: A Lightning Witness for Schools and Clinics: A $91 Sferics and Electric-Field Warning Node, Its Computed Warning-Time Budget, and the Limits of the 30-30 Rule
explanation: Lightning is fatal to an estimated 6,000–24,000 people per year worldwide and injures roughly ten times as many, with schools, clinics, and sports fields in regions without warning infrastructure among the recurring sites of multiple-casualty incidents. The guidance such institutions actually use, the 30–30 rule, is reactive: it can only trigger after a cloud-to-ground (CG) strike close enough to hear has already occurred.

name: A Disaster Mesh Communications Budget for a Town Without Grid or Towers: Coverage, Traffic, Power and Price for the First Week
explanation: A solar-relay mesh kit — relays plus a handset per household — that keeps a town coordinating when grid and towers fail. It serves emergency-communications suppliers and municipalities.

name: A Corrected Low-Cost Indoor Particle Witness: Humidity, Coincidence and Scattering Corrections for Classification Against the WHO 24-Hour PM2.5 Guideline, Below US$60
explanation: A low-cost air-quality sensor paired with a correction method for the humidity and coincidence errors that make cheap sensors misclassify air. It serves air-quality instrument makers and school and clinic suppliers.

name: A Post-Disaster Power Triage Kit for a Small Clinic: Load Definition, Photovoltaic and Battery Sizing, and Load-Shedding Rules
explanation: When the grid fails, a small clinic loses refrigeration, light, communications and powered medical devices at the same time. This blueprint specifies a photovoltaic and battery kit governed by explicit load-shedding rules: 2.8 kW of photovoltaic modules and 14.4 kWh (nameplate) of lithium iron phosphate storage, costing US$10,070, massing 360 kg and packing into 1.39 m3.

name: Earthquake Early Warning from Cheap Accelerometers: An Honest Latency-and-Geometry Budget, a Blind Zone, and a Priced Verdict
explanation: Earthquake early warning systems exist in a small number of wealthy countries, because the seismometers they were built on are expensive. Most earthquake deaths occur in regions with no early warning system.

name: A Passive Indoor Radon Witness Cheap Enough to Matter: Design and Fully Computed Sensitivity Budget for a 90-Day CR-39 Diffusion-Chamber Detector at Under US$5 in Parts
explanation: A 90-day passive radon test built on a CR-39 witness element, with $4.75 in parts, priced as a product rather than a service. It serves test-kit manufacturers and home-inspection suppliers.

name: A Wildfire-Smoke Refuge Room for a Classroom or Clinic Ward: An Integrated Sizing Law and a Priced Comparison of Box-Fan Filter Arrays and HEPA Purifiers
explanation: This blueprint specifies one room — 180 m³ (10 m × 6 m × 3 m), 30 occupants, suitable as a classroom or a six-bed clinic ward — converted into a clean-air refuge during a multi-day wildfire smoke event, with outdoor fine particulate matter (PM2.5) of 250–600 µg/m³. The room is sized by a well-mixed mass balance.

name: A Heat-Wave Survival Room: The Integrated Design, Computed Cooling Budget and Cost per Protected Person for One Cooled Room per Dwelling
explanation: A room-by-room envelope package that keeps one room survivable through a heat wave where whole-home cooling is unaffordable. It serves municipalities, landlords, and heat-action programs working through building suppliers.

name: A Post-Disaster Drinking-Water Triage Kit for the First 72 Hours: Staged Treatment, Computed Log Removal, Gravity Throughput and a Priced Verdict
explanation: A 1.70 kg gravity-only water kit for the first 72 hours after a disaster, before supply chains restart. It needs no power and no pumps. It serves disaster-relief suppliers, NGOs, and emergency-preparedness retailers.

name: Farm-Scale Electrochemical Ammonia: A Costed Design and Its Failure at Small Scale
explanation: The design paper sets out this design in full: Farm-Scale Electrochemical Ammonia: A Costed Design and Its Failure at Small Scale.

name: Non-Thermal Plasma Nitrogen Fixation at Village Scale: A Computed Design Budget for a Solar-Powered Gliding-Arc Unit, Compared with a Dielectric Barrier Discharge and with Delivered Synthetic Fertiliser
explanation: The design paper sets out this design in full: Non-Thermal Plasma Nitrogen Fixation at Village Scale: A Computed Design Budget for a Solar-Powered Gliding-Arc Unit, Compared with a Dielectric Barrier Discharge and with Delivered Synthetic Fertiliser.

name: Small-Scale Compressed-Air Energy Storage for a Village or Workshop: A First-Principles Design, Efficiency and Cost Test
explanation: The design paper sets out this design in full: Small-Scale Compressed-Air Energy Storage for a Village or Workshop: A First-Principles Design, Efficiency and Cost Test. Loses to lithium iron phosphate except where a tested pressure vessel already exists.

name: Building-Scale Gravity Energy Storage for Off-Grid Homes: A First-Principles Design and Cost Test
explanation: The design paper sets out this design in full: Building-Scale Gravity Energy Storage for Off-Grid Homes: A First-Principles Design and Cost Test.

name: Thermochemical Heat Storage for Homes: A Strontium Bromide Seasonal Store Designed From First Principles
explanation: The design paper sets out this design in full: Thermochemical Heat Storage for Homes: A Strontium Bromide Seasonal Store Designed From First Principles.

name: Water as a Seasonal Heat Store: A First-Principles Design for Half of a Cold-Climate Winter, Its Six-Month Loss, and the Scale at Which the Loss Becomes Acceptable
explanation: The design paper sets out this design in full: Water as a Seasonal Heat Store: A First-Principles Design for Half of a Cold-Climate Winter, Its Six-Month Loss, and the Scale at Which the Loss Becomes Acceptable.

name: Counter-Rotating Vertical-Axis Wind Turbine Arrays: Designing Against the Spacing Tax from the Other Side
explanation: A counter-rotating vertical-axis turbine array designed for small sites that cannot use large-turbine spacing rules; the array's interaction physics is its own design subject. It serves small-wind makers supplying sites — farms, compounds, small industrial plots — where large-turbine spacing rules do not fit.

name: Programmable White Blood Cells: A Two-Marker Specificity-Logic Design for Engineered T Cells
explanation: An engineered T-cell design that activates only when two independent disease markers are present together — a logic AND gate computed inside the living therapeutic cell, so the therapy itself decides where it may act. It is research-stage work for cell-therapy firms, licensed by indication field with milestone structure and no product claims.

name: DNA as a Data-Storage Chip: A Full Architecture and Computed Performance Budget for an Archival Storage Device
explanation: A complete hybrid DNA data-storage architecture — write path, cartridge, read path, and error-correction budget — specified end to end rather than as a laboratory demonstration of one step. It serves archival-storage technology firms and data-centre operators holding records that must outlive every current medium.

name: DNA Strand-Displacement Computing for Molecular Diagnostics: A Design Study of a Pancreatic Cancer Signature Classifier in a Drop of Blood
explanation: A molecular circuit that runs in the sample itself and classifies a four-marker pancreatic-cancer signature in a drop of blood, needing no instrument. The circuit computes (miR-21 AND miR-196a) AND (CA19-9 OR KRAS G12D). It is research-stage work for molecular-diagnostics firms.

name: Cell-Free DNA Circuits as the Safer Injectable: A Design Study of a Marker-Activated Molecular System Without Living Cells
explanation: A DNA-only molecular system, inert until two disease markers unlock it inside a cell, that then acts and clears from the body in about a day. No living cells are involved. It is research-stage work for molecular-therapeutics firms, licensed by field with milestone structure.

name: A Range-Certified Electro-Optical Observation Station
explanation: A bearing-only camera cannot certify the physical size, transverse velocity, or transverse acceleration of an observed object, because every bearing observable depends only on ratios of those quantities to range. The source certification result established this non-identifiability formally and showed that one independent range channel closes the error budget.

name: A Range-Certified Observation Station, Version 2: Thermal Channels, Automated Tracking, Catalogue Cross-Match, and a Fused Two-Node Trajectory Budget
explanation: A two-node observation station with thermal cameras and automated tracking. Its readings are cross-checked automatically against the satellite catalogue and aircraft broadcasts, so the station certifies what its cameras saw rather than merely recording it. It serves airfields, critical-infrastructure perimeters, and research organisations — including observation research programs — that must defend their data.

name: Sizing the Walls of a Low-Cost Insulated Fish Box: Expanded Polystyrene versus a Sawdust-Filled Double Wooden Wall
territory: Fishing and Small Boats
explanation: An insulated fish box is usually built with whatever sheet insulation is at hand, at whatever thickness fits, and its performance is discovered on the first hot trip. This paper instead sizes the walls from a stated duty: a box of fixed external size 1.00 m × 0.60 m × 0.60 m must hold 40 kg of fish, loaded at 5 °C, with a 25 kg ice charge, at or below 4 °C for 48 hours at an ambient temperature of 35 °C.

name: A Waiting Rule for Newly Anchored Fish Aggregating Devices: How Long a New Device Must Stand Before Fishing It, with a Mooring Scope and Anchor Table
territory: Fishing and Small Boats
explanation: A fish aggregating device, a moored raft or buoy under which fish gather, does not fish at full strength on the day it is anchored. This paper models the build-up of the aggregation as an approach to a settled level with a time constant of 7 days, a stated assumption informed qualitatively by published accounts of aggregation behaviour, and turns that curve into a waiting rule.

name: A Degradable Escape Panel Specification for Fish Traps: A Cotton-Twine Fastener That Ends Ghost Fishing Within Thirty Days
territory: Fishing and Small Boats
explanation: A lost fish trap does not stop fishing. Its bait draws a first catch, the catch itself becomes bait for the next, and the trap can go on taking fish long after its owner has written it off.

name: Sizing the Outrigger Float of a Single-Outrigger Canoe: Ama Volume, Crossbeam Length and Heel Limits
territory: Fishing and Small Boats
explanation: A single-outrigger canoe depends for most of its stability on one small float, the ama, held away from the hull by a crossbeam. Builders size that float by inheritance and by eye, and the penalty for undersizing is paid in a capsize or in a boat that cannot be worked.

name: A Sizing Rule for Fish Trap Funnel Throats: Throat Diameter and Cone Angle Against Entry and Escape
territory: Fishing and Small Boats
explanation: A trap funnel has to do two opposed things: admit the fish that are wanted and then refuse to let them back out. This study originates a sizing rule for the funnel entrance cone by modelling both duties from stated assumptions.

name: A Salt-Penetration Rule for Whole and Split Fish: Salting Times by Thickness, the Spoilage Thickness Limit, and Dry Salting Compared with Brining
territory: Fishing and Small Boats
explanation: A salting process for whole and split fish: fish thicker than the stated spoilage thickness limit are split before curing, and curing times are taken from the source paper's thickness table for dry salting or for a 15 percent brine. Salt preserves fish only where the salt has actually arrived, and the last place it reaches is the centre of the thickest part.

name: A Winter Stores Bound for the Honey Bee Hive: Insulation, Heat Loss, and the Honey a Colony Must Spend
territory: Bees, Honey and Wax
explanation: A clustered honey bee colony in winter is, in thermal terms, a small heat source inside a thin wooden box, and the honey it eats is the fuel that pays for the heat the box loses. This study computes an upper bound on that fuel bill.

name: Condensation Arithmetic in the Winter Hive: Water Production, Wall Temperature, and Where the Moisture Falls
territory: Bees, Honey and Wax
explanation: A winter colony manufactures water as surely as it manufactures heat: oxidising the sugars in honey yields 0.48 kilograms of metabolic water for every kilogram of honey consumed, so a colony eating 100 grams of honey a day produces 48.0 grams of water a day that must leave the hive as vapour or arrive somewhere as liquid. This study computes where that water goes.

name: Summer Heat Load in the Honey Bee Hive: Fanning Bees, Water Demand, and a Roof and Shade Sizing Rule
territory: Bees, Honey and Wax
explanation: A hive summer configuration following the source paper's order of measures: light-coloured finish first, roof insulation second, shade third, with a water supply sized to the computed fanning and evaporation demand. In summer the thermal problem of a hive reverses: the colony must dispose of heat rather than conserve it, and it pays for cooling in water fetched by foragers and in bees diverted to fanning.

name: A Bait Hive Sized by Arithmetic: A Capture-Odds Model and the Cheapest Specification That Reaches a Stated Probability
territory: Bees, Honey and Wax
explanation: A bait hive built to the cheapest specification in the source paper that reaches the stated swarm-capture probability, including its volume, entrance and placement terms. Bait hives, empty boxes set out to attract honey bee swarms, are usually built by copying a traditional size without asking how much each feature contributes or what a cheaper box gives up.

name: Wax Rendering, Weighed Honestly: Mass Balance, Method Losses, and a Solar Melter Sizing Rule
territory: Bees, Honey and Wax
explanation: A solar wax melter sized by the source paper's rule, with the rendering mass balance and method losses stated there used as the operating budget. Rendering beeswax is usually discussed in the language of craft habit rather than arithmetic, and one habit in particular has survived for decades: the claim that old brood comb renders about half its weight in clean wax.

name: The Counterweight Well: Sizing the Stone That Reduces the Work of Raising Water
territory: Wells, Hand Pumps and Rope
explanation: A counterbalanced bucket lift hangs a stone on the far side of the rope, so that the operator raises the bucket and its water against only the difference between their weight and the stone's, and the stone then helps to bring the empty bucket back down. This design study performs the full energy accounting for such a device over a complete cycle, including the return stroke, which casual treatments omit.

name: Sizing the Cylinder to the Well: A Force-Balance Rule for Hand-Pump Bore Diameter Against Depth
territory: Wells, Hand Pumps and Rope
explanation: A hand pump asks one person to lift, on every upstroke, the entire column of water standing above its piston. That simple fact places a hard ceiling on how wide the cylinder bore may be for a given depth of water, yet bore diameters are commonly chosen from what is available, what a neighbouring installation uses, or what a supplier stocks, rather than from the force the operator can actually deliver.

name: What the Earth Asks of a Well Lining: Lateral Pressure, Ring Load, and a Thickness Rule
territory: Wells, Hand Pumps and Rope
explanation: A circular lining in a hand-dug well works mainly in hoop compression: the ground presses inward on the ring, and the ring carries that pressure by squeezing itself. This paper computes the inward pressure by depth for four stated soil classes, using at-rest earth pressure above a stated water table at 10 m and adding full hydrostatic pressure below it.

name: The Rope Pump Depth Bound: Slip, Washer Spacing, and the Depth at Which Output Falls Away
territory: Wells, Hand Pumps and Rope
explanation: A rope pump lifts water on an endless rope carrying washers through a rising main, and it is sometimes described as though depth were a secondary consideration. This study models a rope pump under stated assumptions, with a rising main of inner diameter 0.040 m, washers of diameter 0.038 m, a rope speed of 0.70 m/s, and washer spacing of 0.20 m, giving an ideal displacement of 3.167 m^3/h.

name: Two Legs Against the Head: Discharge Bounds for the Treadle Pump by Depth
territory: Wells, Hand Pumps and Rope
explanation: A treadle pump is driven by the legs and body weight of a standing operator, and its usefulness for household supply and garden irrigation depends on how its discharge falls as the suction head grows. This study models a two-cylinder treadle pump under stated assumptions: a sustainable treadling power of 75 W, an overall efficiency of 0.62 giving 46.5 W of hydraulic power, and a displacement cap of 4.283 m^3/h set by the cylinder geometry and treadling rate.

name: Three Legs and a Load: Buckling, Splay Angle, and the Safe Load of a Well-Digging Tripod
territory: Wells, Hand Pumps and Rope
explanation: A tripod of three wooden poles, lashed at the top and splayed over the mouth of a well, is the lifting structure most often available where a well is dug or a pump is serviced by hand.

name: The Windlass Wind-Up: Drum Diameter, Rope Layers, and the True Effort of Raising a Bucket
territory: Wells, Hand Pumps and Rope
explanation: A hand windlass is usually sized as though the rope wrapped on the bare drum, so that the effort is set by the core radius for the whole lift. In service the rope stacks in layers, each new layer winding onto a larger radius than the layer beneath it, and the torque demanded at the crank grows accordingly.

name: Bad Air at the Bottom: A Ventilation Bound and a Test Rule for Hand-Dug Wells
territory: Wells, Hand Pumps and Rope
explanation: A deployable procedure for hand-dug wells: ventilate and test the air at the bottom by the source paper's test rule before and during work below ground. Carbon dioxide is denser than air, is produced continuously by a person working hard, and can accumulate in an unventilated shaft faster than intuition suggests.

name: Lime and Ash: What a Wood-Ash Pozzolan Mortar Can and Cannot Do
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: A mortar of lime and rice husk ash at 1:2, moist-cured, honestly claimed at M2.5 (2.96 MPa at 28 days in simulation), and not used below ground or in standing water. Wood-ash-only and ash-clay mixes in the source paper do not meet their claimed strengths and are not specified here.

name: How Far Can a Bamboo Culm Span? Bending Strength and Deflection Bounds for Single and Bundled Culms
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: Bamboo culm beams, single or bundled, spanning only within the deflection-governed bounds in the source paper for the stated loads. Bamboo culms are used as rafters, purlins, and joists in a great deal of the world's building, and the question a builder actually asks — how far can this culm reach before it is overstressed or sags too much — is usually answered by tradition rather than by number.

name: The Bamboo Column Bound: Safe Axial Load by Culm Diameter, Wall Thickness, and Node Spacing
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: A bamboo culm used as a post is usually sized by habit: a thick culm for a heavy roof, a thin one for a light wall, with no number attached to either choice. This paper replaces habit with a computed bound.

name: A Bolt Through a Bamboo Culm Does Not Use the Culm's Strength: Splitting and Bearing Bounds at Pinned Joints, and a Lashing Rule That Does
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: A bolted bamboo joint detailed so bearing and splitting at the pin stay within the bounds computed in the source paper. Bolting is the connection method a builder trained on timber or steel reaches for first, and in bamboo it is applied with an expectation this paper tests and disproves by arithmetic: that a bolted joint transfers something like the culm's own strength.

name: The Dry-Stone Retaining Wall Bound: Batter, Base Thickness, and the Height a Vertical Face Cannot Reach
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: A dry-stone retaining wall built with the batter and base thickness given in the source paper for its height, not as a vertical face beyond the computed reach. Dry-stone retaining walls are traditionally built with a batter — the face leaning back into the hill — and traditionally defended by assertion.

name: Foundation Width from the Ground Up: A Bearing Rule for Stone Strip Footings
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: A stone wall is heavy enough that its foundation is a calculation, not a detail, yet footing widths are still commonly chosen as the wall's thickness plus a hand's breadth, whatever the ground. This paper builds the width from the ground up.

name: The Honest Load of a Green-Timber Lintel: Strength Loss and Creep in Unseasoned Wood
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: An unseasoned timber lintel loaded only to the reduced strength, with the creep allowance, computed in the source paper. Builders frequently install a lintel green — freshly sawn, still wet — and then load it with the wall it was meant to carry, while the only capacity figures at hand come from tables for seasoned timber.

name: Lashed, Pegged, or Notched: Computed Strengths for Timber Joints Without Metal, and a Selection Rule
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: Timber joints made by lashing, pegging or notching, each used only up to the computed strength and under the selection rule in the source paper. Timber can be joined without any metal at all, by lashing members together with rope, by driving wooden pegs through them, or by cutting one member to fit into a notch in the other.

name: The Round-Log Beam Rule: Span from Diameter for Roof and Floor Loads
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: A round log used whole, without sawing, is one of the oldest beam forms available to a builder who has trees but no mill. This paper originates a sizing rule for such beams by computing, for a circular cross-section, both the span at which bending strength is exhausted and the span at which sag reaches a stated limit, for two stated load cases and three stated species classes.

name: Mud Brick and Stabilised Earth: Strength by Mix, and the Least Cement or Lime That Does the Work
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: Mud bricks, stabilised where needed with the least cement or lime that the source paper's mix strengths show to do the work. Earth dug on site is the cheapest wall material available in much of the world, and also the least predictable, because two soils that look alike can differ by a factor of two in strength and by far more once rain reaches them.

name: Scaffolds and Formwork from Poles: Safe Loads, Bracing, and the Bay Size That Holds
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: A scaffold and formwork system built from poles, with the bracing and bay size given in the source paper and loaded only to its computed safe loads. Where steel tube scaffolding is unavailable or unaffordable, scaffolds and formwork are built from timber poles lashed or nailed together, and they are usually sized by copying whatever stood last time.

name: Roof Trusses from Poles: Geometry and Member Sizes for Spans from Four to Eight Metres
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: A roof truss built from poles, with the geometry and member sizes given in the source paper for spans from four to eight metres. Where sawn timber is scarce or expensive, roof trusses are often built from round poles — and usually sized by copying whatever stood up last time.

name: Rammed Earth by Layers: Lift Thickness, Compaction Energy, and the Slenderness Bound
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: A rammed earth wall is built one shallow layer at a time, and its quality is decided by choices made hundreds of times a day: how thick each loose layer is spread, how much work is beaten into it, and how wet the soil is when the rammer falls. This paper originates a wall rule connecting those choices to the finished wall.

name: How Thick Must a Rubble Stone Wall Be? A Stability Bound by Height and Mortar
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: A rubble stone wall built to the thickness given in the source paper's stability bound for its height and mortar. How thick a rubble stone wall must be is usually answered by habit: a fixed proportion of the height, the same for a mortared wall as for one laid dry.

name: Thatch Against Rain and Rot: Pitch, Thickness, and Service Life by Material and Climate
territory: Building with Local Materials
explanation: A thatched roof keeps a building dry by a division of labour inside the coat: the outer part may wet and dry with every storm, while an inner layer must stay dry for the life of the roof, because material that stays wet is material that rots. This paper originates a combined design rule that joins the two halves of that bargain in one calculation.

name: Stall Shading and Wilting: How Much Selling Time Shade Buys for Leafy Produce, and When It Pays
territory: The Market Stall
explanation: A shade arrangement over a market stall, applied where the source paper shows shade buys enough selling time for leafy produce to pay for itself. Leafy produce displayed at an open market loses water continuously, and once cumulative loss passes a visible wilting point it becomes difficult or impossible to sell at full price.

name: Display Height and Reach: The Reachable Fraction of a Market Stall and a Stepped Display Rule
territory: The Market Stall
explanation: A flat market table hides much of its own stock. This paper calculates, from stated reach assumptions, what fraction of a flat display lies within a customer's comfortable reach, within a customer's maximum reach, and within a vendor's reach from the opposite side.

name: A Cold Box Sized for One Day of Trading: An Ice Sizing Rule per Kilogram of Produce per Trading Hour
territory: The Market Stall
explanation: A trader selling soft produce from an insulated box must decide each morning how much ice to buy. Too little leaves produce warm; too much ties up cash, space and carrying weight.

name: Checking a Spring Scale With What Is at Hand: A Water-Litre Calibration Method and Its Certified Bound
territory: The Market Stall
explanation: A market vendor who owns no test weights still owns, in effect, a reference mass: a measured litre of water. This paper originates a complete checking procedure based on that reference, and, more importantly, computes an honest bound for what the procedure can certify.

name: A strength test for wood-ash lye without instruments
territory: Household Manufactures
explanation: A deployable test procedure for wood-ash lye strength using the no-instrument method in the source paper, used to grade lye before soap making. Wood-ash lye needs to fall within a narrow concentration band for soap-making, yet the household maker usually has no hydrometer or titration kit.

name: One recipe does not fit every fat
territory: Household Manufactures
explanation: A soap-making process in which the lye quantity is matched to the saponification value of the fat actually in hand, following the source paper's per-fat recipes rather than one recipe for every fat. Household soap recipes are often transmitted as a single quantity of alkali per unit of fat, for use with whatever fat is at hand.

name: Sizing a solar salt pan
territory: Household Manufactures
explanation: A household that can reach the sea often asks a deceptively simple question: how large must a solar salt pan be? This paper derives a sizing rule from a water balance rather than from custom or anecdote.

name: Can a small cane operation fuel itself?
territory: Household Manufactures
explanation: A small cane operation is often assumed to be fuel-self-sufficient because industrial mills burn their own bagasse. This paper tests that assumption at household and village scale, on a single-effect open pan, for a basis of 1000.0 kg of cane.

name: Knowing the endpoint without a thermometer
territory: Household Manufactures
explanation: A deployable endpoint test for syrup making that uses the no-thermometer method in the source paper. Syrup makers working without instruments judge the endpoint by hand: a thread drawn between the fingers, a drop set in cold water, a flake falling from the skimmer, or an egg floated in the pan.

name: A wick selection rule for tallow and beeswax candles
territory: Household Manufactures
explanation: A candle fails in two opposite ways. If the wick is too small for the candle, its flame melts only a narrow well in the centre, the walls never melt, and the flame sinks into a tunnel of its own making.

name: Starch recovery, stage by stage
territory: Household Manufactures
explanation: A starch recovery process run stage by stage as in the source paper, with the recovery expected at each stage stated there. Wet extraction of starch looks simple — grind, wash, settle, dry — yet a large share of the starch in the feedstock never reaches the bag.

name: The fuel bound of a small lime kiln, and a weighing test for completeness
territory: Household Manufactures
explanation: A small lime kiln operated within the source paper's fuel bound, with the weighing test given there used to confirm complete burning. Pure calcium carbonate requires 1.78 MJ per kilogram of stone, or 3.178 MJ per kilogram of quicklime.

name: What a household charcoal filter can and cannot do
territory: Household Manufactures
explanation: A household charcoal filter built and used within the limits the source paper computes for what such a filter can and cannot do. This paper sizes a household charcoal filter for a representative organic contaminant, phenol at 5.0 mg/L, from stated adsorption capacities and a contact-time model, and then applies the same arithmetic to two claims the filter cannot meet.

name: Dose Past the Demand, Then Mind the Calendar: Chlorine, Contact Time, and Re-Dosing for Stored Roof Water
territory: Rain, Roofs and Stormwater
explanation: Households that drink stored roof water are commonly told a single chlorine dose — a fixed number of drops or millilitres per container — with no reference to the water's chlorine demand, the contact time the dose needs, or how long the protection lasts.

name: A Barrier Is a Pump Specification: Hydrostatic Load, Sandbag Count, and Leakage at a Household Flood Door
territory: Rain, Roofs and Stormwater
explanation: Household flood protection is usually sold and discussed as a barrier: a board, a gate, or a wall of sandbags fitted across a doorway.

name: Counted, Not Placed for Symmetry: How Many Downpipes a Roof Actually Needs
territory: Rain, Roofs and Stormwater
explanation: Houses are routinely built with downpipes wherever the elevation looks balanced, and gutters overflow in extreme rain is then blamed on the gutter.

name: The Drip Lands Further Out Than the Trench: Width, Wind, and Impact Energy at an Unguttered Eave
territory: Rain, Roofs and Stormwater
explanation: Buildings without gutters shed their roof water from the eave edge, and the standard remedy for the erosion and splashing that follow is a gravel-filled trench along the wall.

name: One Millimetre for Every Roof? First-Flush Diversion Depth Set by Wash-Off Behaviour
territory: Rain, Roofs and Stormwater
explanation: Rainwater harvesting guides commonly instruct householders to divert the first millimetre of rain from the roof, as if one depth suited every roof.

name: Depth Is a Load Before It Is a Sponge: Substrate Depth, Retention, and the Structural Cap on Green Roofs
territory: Rain, Roofs and Stormwater
explanation: Extensive green roofs are specified by substrate depth, and deeper is routinely sold as better for stormwater.

name: The Level Gutter Is a Sediment Trap: Minimum Fall for Self-Cleansing in a 125 mm Half-Round Gutter
territory: Rain, Roofs and Stormwater
explanation: Builders frequently lay eaves gutters dead level because a level gutter is easier to set out and looks neater, and a persistent trade belief holds that the fall makes no practical difference because rain will find the outlet anyway.

name: Three Hundred Millimetres of What? Ponding Depth Set by Soil Drawdown, Not by the Standard Detail
territory: Rain, Roofs and Stormwater
explanation: Rain gardens are commonly detailed with a standard ponding depth — 300 mm appears in guide after guide — as if the depth were a property of the garden rather than of the soil beneath it.

name: Two Gates for a Soakaway: Storage Scanned Over Storm Durations, and a Recovery Test That Size Cannot Pass
territory: Rain, Roofs and Stormwater
explanation: Soakaways are still frequently sized by folklore — a cubic metre per so many square metres of roof — without reference to the storm durations that actually govern storage.

name: Drawn to Fit the Site, Sized by the Flow: The Length a Grass Swale Needs to Treat Runoff
territory: Rain, Roofs and Stormwater
explanation: Grass swales are drawn on drainage plans as green lines of whatever length the site happens to offer, and credited with pollutant removal as if the credit were automatic.

name: The Screen Sizes the Overflow: Mosquito Mesh, Surcharge Head, and Vent Area on a Covered Rainwater Tank
territory: Rain, Roofs and Stormwater
explanation: A covered rainwater tank needs three openings to behave: an overflow that can discharge the design inflow when the tank is full, a vent that admits air as fast as water is drawn off, and mosquito screening on both, fine enough to exclude insects. Installers habitually size the overflow to match the inlet pipe and fit the screen as an afterthought.

name: Chimney Height for a Downdraft Pottery Kiln: The Draft Pressure Needed and the Height Beyond Which Fuel Use Barely Falls
territory: Clay, Pottery and Kilns
explanation: This paper addresses downdraft kilns that stall, smoke back, or burn unevenly because the chimney provides too little draft.

name: Covered Drying for Green Bricks: How Much Roof per Thousand Bricks Keeps Rain Losses Below Fuel Savings
territory: Clay, Pottery and Kilns
explanation: This paper addresses green bricks ruined by rain during open-air drying in wet seasons.

name: Ceramic Water Filter Wall Thickness: The Flow and Pathogen-Removal Trade-Off and a Thickness That Meets Both Targets
territory: Clay, Pottery and Kilns
explanation: This paper addresses households that need a ceramic pot filter which both flows fast enough to be used and removes enough bacteria to be trusted.

name: Rice Husk in Fired Bricks: Why More Husk Is Not Always Better, and the Blend That Best Balances Strength, Weight and Cost
territory: Clay, Pottery and Kilns
explanation: This paper addresses the common belief that adding ever more rice husk to a brick always improves it because the brick becomes lighter and cheaper.

name: Flywheel Sizing for a Human-Powered Potter's Kick Wheel: The Rim Mass That Holds Speed Within a Usable Band While Centring Clay
territory: Clay, Pottery and Kilns
explanation: This paper addresses potter's kick wheels that slow so quickly under the drag of centring clay that the potter must kick constantly and cannot keep both hands on the clay.

name: How Much Insulation Pays in a Small Brick Kiln: A Thickness Rule Balancing Fuel Saved Against Blanket Cost
territory: Clay, Pottery and Kilns
explanation: This paper addresses small updraft and downdraft brick kilns that lose a large share of their fuel heat through uninsulated walls.

name: Sizing a Settling Tank for Washed Clay: The Residence Time That Drops Sand While Keeping Fine Clay in Suspension
territory: Clay, Pottery and Kilns
explanation: This paper addresses washed clay that still contains gritty sand, or that loses its finest and most plastic fraction to the overflow.

name: Cooking Pot Wall Thickness and Thermal Shock: A Lower Bound on Survival Over an Open Flame and an Upper Bound Set by Heating Time
territory: Clay, Pottery and Kilns
explanation: This paper addresses clay cooking pots that crack over an open flame, and heavy pots that survive but take so long to heat that households stop using them.

name: Washing Clay to Prevent Efflorescence: The Number of Wash Cycles That Brings Soluble Salt Below a Visible-Bloom Threshold
territory: Clay, Pottery and Kilns
explanation: This paper addresses white salt bloom appearing on fired bricks and pots made from clay dug near saline ground, spoiling their appearance and weakening mortar bond.

name: Sand Temper and Drying Cracks: The Temper Fraction That Minimises Combined Crack and Strength Losses in Hand-Formed Ware
territory: Clay, Pottery and Kilns
explanation: This paper addresses hand-formed pots that crack while drying when the clay is used untempered, and weaken when too much temper is added.

name: Soak Time at Peak Temperature: The Hold Duration That Minimises the Combined Cost of Fuel and Underfired Rejects
territory: Clay, Pottery and Kilns
explanation: This paper addresses kiln loads in which ware near the cooler zones is underfired when the firing ends as soon as the hottest cone falls.

name: Sun Pre-Drying Bricks Before Firing: The Moisture Content at Which Further Drying Stops Paying in Saved Kiln Fuel
territory: Clay, Pottery and Kilns
explanation: This paper addresses bricks and pots sent into the kiln still holding water that the sun could have removed for free, paid for instead in fuel and in steam damage.

name: Setter Spacing for Flat Roof Tiles: The Support Interval That Keeps Firing Warpage Within a Stated Tolerance
territory: Clay, Pottery and Kilns
explanation: This paper addresses flat clay roof tiles that warp during firing because they are supported too far apart while soft at peak temperature.

name: A Span Limit for Self-Supporting Brick Kiln Vaults: The Width a Catenary Arch of Fired Brick Can Cover Without Steel
territory: Clay, Pottery and Kilns
explanation: This paper addresses kiln builders who want a permanent brick vault roof instead of a rebuilt temporary crown, but have no rule for how wide such a vault can safely span.

name: The Cheapest Cotton and Linen Blend That Meets a Stated Yarn Strength: An Interaction Model and Its Answer
territory: Fibre, Spinning and Weaving
explanation: Blending cotton with linen is usually discussed in the language of character: hand, lustre, drape, coolness.

name: The Drop Spindle Whorl: A Mass Rule That Balances Spin Time Against the Drafter's Arm
territory: Fibre, Spinning and Weaving
explanation: A drop spindle costs almost nothing, yet its one shaped part, the whorl, decides how the tool behaves for every metre of yarn it ever makes. Spinners choose whorls by habit, by what came with the spindle, or by copying a teacher, and trade descriptions ('a fast whorl', 'a long-spinning whorl') circulate without numbers attached.

name: Reusing the Dye Bath: Replenishment Fractions, Shade Drift and the Cycle Count Before the Colour Leaves Tolerance
territory: Fibre, Spinning and Weaving
explanation: A dye bath at the end of its first batch is not exhausted; on the figures dyers themselves quote, a substantial share of the dye is still in the water being poured away. Reusing the bath is standard advice, but the advice usually stops at 'top it up and go again', without saying how much dye to add, how the shade will drift as the bath ages, or how many batches can honestly be sold as the same colour.

name: Sizing a Water Retting Tank for Flax: Litres, Days and Water Changes per Kilogram of Fibre
territory: Fibre, Spinning and Weaving
explanation: Water retting is the step that decides whether flax straw becomes spinnable fibre or compost, and it is usually sized by whatever tank a household happens to own.

name: Cutting the Reed Width Right First Time: A Shrinkage Rule for Cotton, Linen, Wool and Silk Warps
territory: Fibre, Spinning and Weaving
explanation: Cloth leaves the loom narrower than the warp was sleyed, because the weft's crimp relaxes, the warp's tension releases, and the fabric settles into the dimensions it actually wants.

name: The Lay of a Three-Strand Rope: The Helix Angle That Carries the Most Load per Kilogram of Fibre
territory: Fibre, Spinning and Weaving
explanation: A rope is fibre spent along a helix, and the steepness of that helix, the lay, is the rope maker's central compromise. Lay the strands softly and they run nearly parallel to the load, which is efficient, but the rope is limp, easily damaged, and prone to unlaying; lay them hard and the rope is round, stable, and handsome, while a growing share of its fibre points sideways, where it carries nothing, and friction between strands begins to tax what remains.

name: A Cover Rule for Handwoven Shade Cloth: The Widest Tape Spacing That Still Delivers Seventy Percent Shade
territory: Fibre, Spinning and Weaving
explanation: Shade cloth for seedlings is specified by the shade it gives, woven by hand at whatever spacing the weaver's eye approves, and the two descriptions meet only by luck.

name: Choosing a Spinning Wheel Drive Ratio: The Ratio at Which Take-Up, Not Twist, Sets the Pace
territory: Fibre, Spinning and Weaving
explanation: Most spinning wheels are sold with two or three drive ratios, selected by moving the drive band between grooves on the whorl, and most instruction treats the choice as a matter of taste: a high ratio for fine yarn, a low ratio for thick.

name: Weaving a Water Filter Cloth to a Stated Pore Size: The Ends per Inch That Deliver It, and What the Flow Costs
territory: Fibre, Spinning and Weaving
explanation: Woven cloth is the oldest filter medium in the world and still the one a village workshop can make for itself, but a filter is specified by its pore size while a loom is set by thread counts, and the translation between the two is rarely written down.

name: Bed Height for Older Sleepers: The Seat-Height Rule That Minimises Sit-to-Stand Effort, and the Fall Energy Cost of Exceeding It
territory: Sleep, Bedding and the Night Room
explanation: Bed height is usually set by furniture fashion — deep mattresses on high frames — but for an older sleeper the height of the bed's top surface decides both how hard it is to stand up in the morning and how far there is to fall at night.

name: Blackout Is a Gap Problem: Light at the Eye from Blind Edge Leakage as a Function of Gap Width, and the Overlap That Replaces Expensive Fabric
territory: Sleep, Bedding and the Night Room
explanation: Expensive blackout fabric is specified by its transmittance, but the light that reaches a sleeper's eye in a real installation is dominated by the gaps at the edges, not by the fabric.

name: Dawn Simulation, Priced in Lux-Minutes: The Ramp Duration and Peak Illuminance a Wake-Up Light Needs at Realistic Pillow Distances
territory: Sleep, Bedding and the Night Room
explanation: Wake-up lights promise a simulated dawn, but the simulation is delivered at the pillow, and pillow distance is set by furniture, not by the product's specification sheet, which quotes illuminance at a flattering range.

name: The Mosquito Net Trade-Off: Mesh Aperture Against Air Movement, and the Hole Size at Which a Net Stops Cooling the Sleeper It Protects
territory: Sleep, Bedding and the Night Room
explanation: A mosquito net protects by exclusion and penalises by stillness: the finer the mesh, the less air moves under it, and in a hot room the loss of cooling is the price of the bite protection. This paper models air movement through netting as a stated function of its open-area fraction, for apertures from 0.4 to 2.0 mm against a stated thread diameter of 0.25 mm.
